cells.tense: Right now you are reading what is arriving and adjusting the mix without losing your footing.
cells.act: teach it the way it was taught to you, with one change
cells.ask: Show a thing you already do well to somebody who hasn't learned it, the way it first came to you — then change one step so it fits them. Watch the change hold.
cells.core:
Something is arriving and you can meet it without deciding anything about it yet. You read what's coming, you adjust what you're carrying, and the adjustment doesn't cost you your footing. A lot of people meet a new thing by picking a side early. You meet it level, and you let the mix tell you what it needs.

This week there's a thing you'll want to hand to somebody else. Hand it over the way it first came to you, then change one step to fit who they are — the small change you'd make without thinking. Notice that change is yours. That's the part that doesn't get recorded, and it's what the next person inherits.
cells.sheetLine: You can meet what arrives without picking a side early.
cells.verb: calibrating the mix as it arrives
cells.place: the threshold where what is coming in first meets you

cells.tense: You are smoothing what is arriving before it has had a chance to land, and the smoothing is becoming the whole job.
cells.ask: Take a first step today or tomorrow toward the thing you have been keeping level — before it feels settled. No announcement needed. Just move while it's still rough.
cells.core:
What is arriving is being brought into agreement before anyone has had a chance to disagree. Every new thing gets blended until the surface is flat, and you can do that so well that nobody notices the surface is the point. It feels like keeping the peace. What it costs is that nothing new enters as itself — it enters already adjusted, already welcome, already the same as what was there.

There is something you want that you have not moved toward. Take the first step toward it before the room is ready for it. Not a confrontation — a direction. You know which one. Moving toward it while it's still rough is what lets the mix actually balance, instead of pretending it already has.
cells.sheetLine: You're smoothing what arrives before it ever lands.
cells.verb: calibrating the mix as it arrives
cells.place: the threshold where what is coming in first meets you

cells.tense: You are standing at a door that has already opened, and you are still reading the wood for signs of what's coming.
cells.act: stay in contact while it is hard
cells.ask: Next time someone you already talk to is in something hard, stay in the conversation one exchange longer than feels natural — past where you'd normally go quiet or reach for a fix.
cells.core:
The center is not where you are standing. Every new thing that arrives gets reacted to as if it's the same shape as the last one, and there's no steady place left to read from, so the reading skips straight to the reaction. You're still arriving places — you just arrive braced, and the brace is what meets whoever's there. The door opened already.

Stay with one person a little longer than you usually would when they are in something hard. Not to fix it, not to say the right thing — just stay in the conversation one exchange past where you would normally pull back. The staying is what rebuilds the center. It doesn't come back through thinking about it; it comes back through contact.
cells.sheetLine: You arrive braced, and the brace is what people meet.
cells.verb: calibrating the mix as it arrives
cells.place: the threshold where what is coming in first meets you

cells.tense: You are already adjusting to what is arriving and you have been calling it something that isn't the adjusting.
cells.act: learn how the people before you did it
cells.ask: Ask somebody who has done the thing longer than you how they first learned it. Listen for the part that surprises you. Carry it with you — no notes.
cells.core:
You're tuning what comes in — trimming here, adding there, finding the level — and the tuning is being filed under luck or under the moment. You haven't been calling it a skill. It is one, and it's the kind that gets passed person to person, not put on paper. The ones near you are getting the benefit and the credit doesn't have your name on it, and you'd probably say that's fine.

Find one person who's been doing what you do longer than you have, and ask how they first learned it. Listen for the part that surprises you — the thing you wouldn't have guessed. That's the part that tells you your own adjustments came from somewhere, and that you're making new ones on top. Ask the question and leave the answer where it sits; you'll know it landed when you catch yourself doing the thing differently the next day.
cells.sheetLine: You've been calling your tuning luck.
cells.verb: calibrating the mix as it arrives
cells.place: the threshold where what is coming in first meets you

The asks survive being wrong: each is a small act from the medicine's own list, useful whether or not the read lands. The Unacknowledged ask uses the Culture reduction (learn how the people before you did it — the simpler earlier form of the same line) rather than the full transmission acts; the record's REDUCTION mechanism wants the earlier form.
